IP-activity tags compare authors and their institutions with the patent reading list above; a name counts only when the institution matches too, so people who have changed institutions aren't flagged.           How the planner works

          • Ions: ions across the three sites. The common ones (Cs, MA, FA; Pb, Sn; I, Br, Cl) are always shown; use the "Add" menus for the rest. Device counts in the menus are compositions in the Perovskite Database that include the ion.
          • Band gap: for the eight common ions, a quadratic ridge regression on their site fractions, trained on the median band gap reported for each of compositions (5-fold cross-validated error about eV). For any other ion, a model that describes ions by their properties (electronegativity, row, lone pair, charge, size, empty sites, spacer share) instead of their names: a straight-line halide trend plus the three most similar compositions with a known gap. It learns from compositions: the database's 3D, double, vacancy-ordered and layered 2D entries, plus inorganic compounds with gaps measured by Zhuo, Mansouri Tehrani & Brgoch (2018). Tested by hiding every composition containing an ion and predicting them, its error is about eV close to known compositions and – eV farther away. Compositions it can't describe (more than 10% of the X-site sulfide, selenide or fluoride) or that sit far from its data go to a broader, rougher model (new in 1.6) that sees only the metals and anions: it adds measured metal halides, sulfides, selenides, tellurides and chalcohalides from the same compilation, and its error, measured by hiding each element in turn, is about eV next to known chemistry and up to eV far out. Molecular anions above 10% of the X-site, and compositions beyond what either model was tested on, get no estimate and a reason. Every estimate is for a single phase of the composition. Most gaps in the database were assigned from the composition rather than measured, so both models reflect the literature's consensus.
          • Layered 2D perovskites: a large spacer cation (PEA⁺, BA⁺ and six others) splits the perovskite into slabs n octahedra thick. The spacer's share of the A-site fixes n (share = 2 / (n + 1), so 50% is n = 3), and the planner estimates the gap from it. Spacers are treated as interchangeable, so these estimates carry about ± eV wherever they fall.
          • Combinations that can't exist: some ions react with each other, whatever the charges say: borohydride with ammonium-type cations (hydrogen is released) or with easily reduced metals, copper(I) with fluoride, and copper(II) as the main metal in an iodide (CuI₂ doesn't exist). The menus grey these out, and sliders at 0% lock, once one partner is present; "Why are some options greyed out?" under each menu gives the reason.
          • Structure: the charges must add up to zero, so with +1 cations and −1 anions the B-site must average +2. A +3 or +4 metal can still work three ways, which the planner offers as one-click fixes: pair it with a +1 metal (a double perovskite), leave some B-sites empty (a vacancy-ordered compound such as MA₃Bi₂I₉ or Cs₂SnI₆), or swap some halide for a −2 chalcogenide (a chalcohalide). Goldschmidt tolerance factor and octahedral factor use site-averaged radii, and (new in 1.6) each ion is also checked on its own against the other two sites' averages: A-site cations above 5% of their site outside 0.80–1.06, metals above 5% below an octahedral factor of 0.41, and anions above 10% whose radii differ by more than 15% or whose charges differ. When flagged ions make up a fifth of a site, the verdict becomes "Averages hide misfits". "Fits" means 0.86–0.98, "near the edge" means 0.80–0.86 or 0.98–1.06. Radii: Shannon (1976) for inorganic ions (Sn²⁺ 1.10 Å is an estimate); Kieslich, Sun & Cheetham (2014, 2015) for molecular ions. Ions without a tabulated radius, and empty sites, are left out of the factors.
          • Evidence: distance between site-fraction vectors; "close" means within 0.10. Related compounds that use the same ions in a different structure (such as MA₃Bi₂I₉) are listed but not counted. Top 5% is used instead of the single best value because the database contains a few impossible entries. Additive counts are approximate text matches.
          • Lifetime: Kaplan–Meier median hours until efficiency falls to 80%, grouped by the B-site metals and the test atmosphere, counting devices that outlasted their tests. A median is shown only for groups with at least 10 tests.
          • Raw materials: 500 nm film, pseudo-cubic lattice set by the X-site radius (fitted to 6.31, 5.93 and 5.68 Å for iodide, bromide and chloride). Prices and producer shares: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, at the grade USGS reports. Cesium and rubidium have no commodity price; their research-grade prices are shown separately. Organic cations and abundant elements are not priced.
          • Patents: a reading list of patents and applications checked on Google Patents in , each recorded with the ions its formula names, any ranges it states, its written-out examples and the band-gap roles it targets. Matches weigh how much of each site uses ions the patent names, whether its key ions are present, whether the composition sits inside a stated range, how close it is to an example, and whether it targets the same role. Each band-gap role in the legend opens the patents aimed at it. This is not a patent search or a freedom-to-operate opinion.
          • Recent papers: a keyword search of OpenAlex, a free index of scholarly papers, for articles from the last three years that mention the composition (its formula when it's a whole-number one, otherwise its ions). Papers whose authors or institutions also appear on the patent reading list are tagged as IP activity, a hint that the group files patents in the space.
          • Vibrations: lattice vibrations follow the sliders. The page computes them from the force constants of pure compounds (cubic ABX₃ with A = Cs, Rb or K and B = Pb, Sn or Ge, plus Cs with 13 more +2 metals; Cs₂B⁺B³⁺X₆ double perovskites with B⁺ = Ag or Na and B³⁺ = Bi, In or Sb; and vacancy-ordered Cs₂BX₆ with B = Sn⁴⁺, Ti⁴⁺ or Te⁴⁺; X = I, Br, Cl throughout), each from the MACE-MPA-0 machine-learning interatomic potential with phonopy finite displacements in 288- to 320-atom supercells. Mixtures are a virtual crystal: each site becomes one average atom, with masses and force constants averaged by site fraction. Tested against explicit disordered mixed crystals, this is off by cm⁻¹ per mode on average, about 40% less error than using the nearest pure compound, though it misses the separate stretching bands of mixed halides. Organic A-site cations are computed as Cs in the lattice tab, and so are Rb and K where they meet a metal or structure computed only with Cs. Every molecular cation on the menu has its own tab with its normal modes as an isolated ion (B3LYP/6-31G(d), scaled by 0.9614; automatic descriptions for all but MA⁺ and FA⁺), and the cations small enough for a three-dimensional cage can also be shown inside one (new in 1.6): MA⁺, FA⁺, GU⁺ and NH₄⁺ in lead, tin or germanium halide cages, EA⁺, DMA⁺, AZ⁺ and IM⁺ in lead halide cages. TMA⁺ was tried too, but it pulls the lead halide octahedra apart. Each is one pseudo-cubic cell with the cation in a fixed, relaxed orientation, from the same potential, blended over the metals and halides like the lattice. The long spacer cations lie between sheets of octahedra rather than in a cage, so they're shown as free ions. Other ions under 10% of their site are left out; compositions that still can't be modelled say why. Checked against Raman spectra of two double perovskites, the computed frequencies run about % low. Measured Raman, infrared, terahertz and emission-linewidth values come from eight published studies and are listed with each composition.
          • Out of scope: additives, divalent-spacer (Dion–Jacobson) 2D phases, oxides and other all-chalcogenide perovskites, and device-specific efficiency or lifetime predictions.
